query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Plasma nitriding of Ti-6Al-4V alloy using a mixed ammonia/nitrogen atmosphere (with a NH3:N2 ratio of 1:2) at a low temperature (around 750 °C for 4 hours) increases surface hardness and improves wear resistance by forming a thicker, well-adhered nitride compound layer (rich in TiN and Ti2N) compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Ti-6Al-4V alloy with a Widmanstätten microstructure and relatively low surface hardness.
generation.intervention: Apply low-temperature plasma nitriding in a mixed NH3/N2 gas atmosphere (NH3:N2 = 1:2) at 750 °C for 4 hours.
generation.conditions: Tested under tribological conditions such as pin-on-disc or ball-on-disk sliding wear experiments at moderate load and ambient or dry conditions representative of structural service, where the improved surface properties are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase nitride surface consisting of a surface compound layer (δ-TiN and ε-Ti2N) and an underlying diffusion zone, which together introduce compressive residual stresses and a barrier to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Nitrogen incorporation during plasma nitriding reacts with titanium to form hard nitride compounds. These compounds increase the surface hardness and create compressive stresses that delay crack nucleation and reduce abrasive wear, thereby enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nitrided specimens will exhibit a significant increase in microhardness (potentially 3-4 times higher than the untreated substrate) and a substantial reduction in wear loss during standardized wear tests compared to untreated Ti-6Al-4V specimens.
generation.baseline: Untreated Ti-6Al-4V alloy, which typically has a lower hardness (around 400–500 HV) and higher wear rate under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under controlled nitriding parameters; however, if excessive surface roughness or premature crack initiation occurs (especially at higher applied stresses or different nitriding temperatures), the beneficial effects might be negated. The optimal balance between increased hardness and surface roughness is crucial.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the magnitude of wear-resistance improvement under different loading conditions and the extent to which increased surface roughness might offset the hardness gains. Further optimization of nitriding parameters may be required for different application environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti-6Al-4V alloy specimens. Process one set using plasma nitriding with a mixed NH3/N2 atmosphere (ratio 1:2) at 750 °C for 4 hours. Keep the other set as the untreated control. Characterize both sets by measuring surface microhardness (using Vickers testing) and performing standardized pin-on-disc wear tests under identical load, speed, and environmental conditions. Additionally, use SEM to examine the nitride layer thickness and integrity.
measurements: Vickers microhardness values at the surface and below the nitrided layer
Wear volume or weight loss from the pin-on-disc tests
SEM images to assess layer thickness, uniformity, and presence of cracks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrided specimens do not show a statistically significant increase in surface hardness (e.g., less than a 2-fold increase) and a corresponding reduction in wear (no significant decrease in wear volume/weight loss) compared to the untreated control, or if the nitride layer shows extensive cracking or delamination leading to poor performance, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Owing to their superior mechanical properties, low density, and excellent corrosion resistance, titanium alloys find extensive applications across various industries, including the aerospace, medical, automotive, and industrial sectors. However, their low hardness and poor tribological characteristics constrain their broader utilization. Despite the inherently low hardness and wear resistance of titanium and its alloys, Ti-N (TiN and Ti2N) compounds exhibit high hardness, chemical stability, and wear resistance. Consequently, surface modification techniques are frequently utilized to deposit a Ti-N compound layer on these materials, thereby enhancing their hardness, wear resistance, and even corrosion resistance. The Ti-N compound layer serves as a protective barrier, reducing friction and wear by impeding direct contact between the alloy surface and the contacting material [,]. This results in enhanced durability and wear resistance, which is particularly advantageous in applications where the material is exposed to repetitive or high-load contacts. The growth of the Ti-N compound layer was enhanced by the use of an NH3-N2 mixture during the plasma nitriding of the Ti6Al4V alloy. After nitriding at 750 °C for 4 h in an NH3-N2 (1:2) atmosphere, a Ti-N compound layer approximately 2 μm thick was formed on the Ti6Al4V alloy. The Ti-N compound layers are typically much harder than the titanium alloy substrate. In comparison to the un-nitrided titanium alloy, samples nitrided in an NH3-N2 mixture exhibited the complete elimination of stick–tear and plowing wear throughout the duration of the test, resulting in undetectable wear loss when in contact with bearing steel. The oxide layer formed on the wear track by the transfer of material from the counterpart steel ball reduced the average friction coefficient from approximately 0.55 to 0.30 under an 8N load. The formation of the Ti-N layer not only enhances the hardness and wear resistance of the titanium alloy but also increases its corrosion resistance.

By varying the microstructure and nitriding parameters, the fatigue strength of a material can be affected. Tokaji et al. [] reported that the fatigue strength of pure titanium was increased by nitriding, while it was decreased in the case of Ti-6Al-4V. Based on detailed observations of fatigue crack initiation, growth, and fracture surfaces, the improvement and the reduction in fatigue strength by nitriding of pure titanium and Ti-6Al-4V alloys were primarily attributed to enhanced crack initiation resistance and to premature crack initiation of the nitride layer, respectively. However, Farokhzadeh et al. [] achieved an improvement on the fatigue proprieties of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy plasma nitrided at a low temperature (600 °C). These results were different than those obtained by an elevated temperature treatment (900 °C) as well as conventional gas/plasma nitriding treatments reported in the literature [,,]. The thin morphology of the compound layer restricted the extent of premature crack initiation from the surface. Increased fatigue life of the plasma nitrided specimens in tests at higher stresses can be attributed to compressive residual stress in the nitride layers and in the nitrogen diffusion zone, thereby inhibiting crack nucleation at the alloy surface. This is in agreement with another study by Rodriguez et al. []. According to Farokhzadeh et al. [], the nitride layer reduces the extent of brittle failure on the specimen surface while the diffusion zone provides mechanical support. As per the study of Morita et al [], the formation of these layers after plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of the alloy, which in turn increases the resistance to movement of dislocations and, as a consequence, increases the fatigue strength of the alloy. Rocha [], reported that delay in crack nucleation in plasma nitrided specimens is due to the difference in the Young modulus between the titanium alloy matrix (100 GPa) and the titanium nitrides formed on the plasma nitride surface (400 GPa). When high stresses are applied to the fragile nitride layer, it causes the nucleation and the growth of a crack in this layer.
